analysis.one_liner: Ends surprise air-ambulance bills by capping patient costs at in-network rates.
analysis.headline: A bill to stop surprise air-ambulance bills was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, never got a hearing or vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: When someone is badly hurt and flown to a hospital by helicopter, the flight is often run by a company the patient's insurance doesn't cover. The patient never chose that company, and afterward can get a bill for tens of thousands of dollars beyond what insurance pays. This bill would have said patients pay only the normal in-network cost for emergency air ambulance flights, and set up an arbitration process to decide what the insurer pays the flight company.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who needs an emergency air ambulance flight and has private health insurance. Patients would pay no more than the in-network cost of the flight, that amount would count toward their deductible, and air ambulance companies could not bill them for anything beyond it unless they had signed a written agreement at least 24 hours beforehand — which is nearly impossible in an emergency.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insured patients facing emergency air-ambulance bills

how_it_helps.text: Health plans could not charge a patient more for an out-of-network air ambulance flight than they would for an in-network one, and the patient's share must count toward their deductible [S2] [S3].

The insurer would pay the air ambulance company the rate set by state law where it operates, or where none exists, a rate set through an independent arbitration process between the insurer and the flight company [S2] [S3].
An air ambulance company that billed a patient above that cost-share, without signed informed consent, would face a federal civil penalty [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private air ambulance companies, which currently can charge whatever they want on emergency flights and bill patients for the balance. Insurers would pay capped, benchmark-based rates instead of sky-high out-of-network charges.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private air ambulance companies; insurers pay benchmark rates

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only patients in the group and individual insurance markets. It does not cap what air ambulance companies charge Medicare and Medicaid, which cover a large share of rural patients, or people with no insurance at all.

Air ambulance companies argue their high charges reflect the cost of keeping crews and helicopters on standby in low-population areas, and that paying benchmark rates negotiated for hospitals could push some rural services to shut down. Independent arbitration based on comparable local rates was designed to blunt that, but the concern is real for a capital-intensive service [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and targeted: an unexpected helicopter flight can leave a patient with a five-figure bill for a service they had no way to choose or refuse. The design is sensible — it protects the patient, routes the payment fight between insurer and provider into arbitration instead of the patient's mailbox, and allows genuine non-emergency flights to be exempted with written consent. Its main limits are scope: it leaves uninsured people and Medicare and Medicaid patients uncovered, and it does nothing to fix the underlying economics of rural air medical services.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in July 2019 and then to its Health Subcommittee, which never scheduled a hearing or vote, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Neguse introduced the bill on July 16, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1] [S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no further action was ever taken on it [S5].
It had one cosponsor in the 231-member House Democratic caucus and no Republican cosponsors [S4].

Six months after this bill stalled, Congress passed a much broader surprise-billing law, the No Surprises Act, which protects patients from air ambulance balance bills but left the question of what insurers must pay air ambulance companies to regulators to decide later.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private air ambulance companies, which kept the ability to charge emergency patients tens of thousands of dollars above their insurance coverage for at least two more years, until the broader No Surprises Act limited patient cost-sharing in 2022.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Air ambulance companies, until the 2022 federal law

for.name: Rep. Joe Neguse
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill; referred it to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over health billing rules
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and referred it to its Health Subcommittee; never held a hearing or markup on it.

against.name: Air ambulance industry
against.role: Private helicopter and fixed-wing medical flight operators
against.what_they_did: Operated under a payment system, backed by federal preemption of state regulation, that let emergency flight operators charge patients above insurance rates; opposed the arbitration benchmarks in federal surprise-billing negotiations.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no party split was recorded; its two supporters were both Democrats and it drew no Republican cosponsors [S4].

industries.note: These companies charge what the market allows on emergency flights and bill patients for the balance; under the bill, patients would pay only the in-network cost-share and operators would have to accept a state or arbitration-set rate. Several major operators are owned by private equity firms whose returns depend on these payments.
Insurers would pay capped benchmark rates instead of inflated out-of-network charges, and their members would no longer face five-figure surprise bills.

The bill would create a new certified independent dispute resolution process — modeled on entities like the American Arbitration Association — to set payment rates between insurers and flight companies.
